<skill_content name="customize-opencode">
# Skill: customize-opencode

<!--
  Built-in skill. Name and description are registered in code at
  packages/core/src/plugin/skill.ts
  and CUSTOMIZE_OPENCODE_SKILL_DESCRIPTION). The body below becomes the
  skill's content.
-->

# Customizing opencode

opencode validates its own config strictly and refuses to start when a field
is wrong. The shapes below cover the common surface area, but they are a
**summary, not the source of truth**.

## Full schema reference

The authoritative list of every config option — with field types, enums,
defaults, and descriptions — lives in the published JSON Schema:

**<https://opencode.ai/config.json>**

If a field is not documented in this skill, or you need to confirm an exact
shape before writing config, **fetch that URL and read the schema directly**
rather than guessing. opencode hard-fails on invalid config, so the cost of a
wrong shape is a broken startup.

Independently, every `opencode.json` should declare
`"$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json"` so the user's editor catches
mistakes as they type.

## Applying changes

Config is loaded once when opencode starts and is not hot-reloaded. After
saving changes to `opencode.json`, an agent file, a skill, a plugin, or any
other config-time file, **tell the user to quit and restart opencode** for
the changes to take effect. The running session will keep using the
already-loaded config until then.

## Where files live

| Scope                         | Path                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Project config                | `./opencode.json`, `./opencode.jsonc`, or `.opencode/opencode.json` (opencode walks up from the cwd to the worktree root) |
| Global config                 | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (NOT `~/.opencode/`)                                                                   |
| Project agents                | `.opencode/agent/<name>.md` or `.opencode/agents/<name>.md`                                                               |
| Global agents                 | `~/.config/opencode/agent(s)/<name>.md`                                                                                   |
| Project commands              | `.opencode/command/<name>.md` or `.opencode/commands/<name>.md`                                                           |
| Global commands               | `~/.config/opencode/command(s)/<name>.md`                                                                                 |
| Project skills                | `.opencode/skill(s)/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                                                      |
| Global skills                 | `~/.config/opencode/skill(s)/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                                             |
| External skills (auto-loaded) | `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                    |

Configs from each scope are deep-merged. Project overrides global. Unknown
top-level keys in `opencode.json` are rejected with `ConfigInvalidError`.

## opencode.json

Every field is optional.

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "username": "string",
  "model": "provider/model-id",
  "small_model": "provider/model-id",
  "default_agent": "agent-name",
  "shell": "/bin/zsh",
  "logLevel": "DEBUG" | "INFO" | "WARN" | "ERROR",
  "share": "manual" | "auto" | "disabled",
  "autoupdate": true | false | "notify",
  "snapshot": true,
  "instructions": ["AGENTS.md", "docs/style.md"],

  "skills": {
    "paths": [".opencode/skills", "/abs/path/to/skills"],
    "urls": ["https://example.com/.well-known/skills/"]
  },

  "references": {
    "docs": {
      "path": "../docs",
      "description": "Use for product behavior and documentation conventions"
    },
    "sdk": {
      "repository": "owner/sdk",
      "branch": "main",
      "description": "Use for SDK implementation details",
      "hidden": true
    }
  },

  "agent": {
    "my-agent": {
      "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6",
      "mode": "subagent",
      "description": "...",
      "permission": { "edit": "deny" }
    }
  },

  "command": {
    "deploy": { "description": "...", "template": "..." }
  },

  "provider": {
    "anthropic": { "options": { "apiKey": "..." } }
  },
  "disabled_providers": ["openai"],
  "enabled_providers": ["anthropic"],

  "mcp": {
    "playwright": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["npx", "-y", "@playwright/mcp"],
      "enabled": true,
      "env": {}
    },
    "remote-thing": {
      "type": "remote",
      "url": "https://...",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ..." }
    }
  },

  "plugin": [
    "opencode-gemini-auth",
    "opencode-foo@1.2.3",
    "./local-plugin.ts",
    ["opencode-bar", { "option": "value" }]
  ],

  "permission": {
    "edit": "deny",
    "bash": { "git *": "allow", "*": "ask" }
  },

  "formatter": false,
  "lsp": false,

  "experimental": {
    "primary_tools": ["edit"],
    "mcp_timeout": 30000
  },

  "tool_output": { "max_lines": 200, "max_bytes": 8192 },

  "compaction": { "auto": true, "tail_turns": 15 }
}
```

Shape notes worth being explicit about:

- `model` always carries a provider prefix: `"anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6"`.
- `skills` is an object with `paths` and/or `urls`, not an array.
- `references` is an object keyed by alias. Each value is a local path, Git repository, or string shorthand.
- `agent` is an object keyed by agent name, not an array.
- `command` is an object keyed by command name, not an array.
- `plugin` is an array of strings or `[name, options]` tuples, not an object.
- `mcp[name].command` is an array of strings, never a single string. `type` is required.
- `permission` is either a string action or an object keyed by tool name.

## Skills

opencode's skill loader scans for `**/SKILL.md` inside skill directories. The
file is named `SKILL.md` exactly, and lives in its own folder named after the
skill:

```
.opencode/skills/my-skill/SKILL.md
```

Frontmatter:

```markdown
---
name: my-skill
description: One sentence covering what this skill does AND when to trigger it. Front-load the literal keywords or filenames the user is likely to say.
---

# My Skill

(skill body in markdown: instructions, examples, references)
```

- `name` is required, lowercase hyphen-separated, up to 64 chars, and matches the folder name.
- `description` is effectively required: skills without one are filtered out and never surfaced to the model. Cover both _what_ the skill does and _when_ to use it. Write in third person ("Use when...", not "I help with..."). Front-load concrete trigger keywords and filenames; gate with "Use ONLY when..." if the skill should stay quiet on adjacent topics.
- Optional: `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata` (string-string map).

Register skills from non-default locations via `skills.paths` (scanned
recursively for `**/SKILL.md`) and `skills.urls` (each URL serves a list of
skills).

## References

References make local directories and Git repositories outside the active
project available as supporting context. Configure them under `references`,
keyed by the alias used in `@` autocomplete:

```json
{
  "references": {
    "docs": {
      "path": "../product-docs",
      "description": "Use for product behavior and terminology"
    },
    "effect": {
      "repository": "Effect-TS/effect",
      "branch": "main",
      "description": "Use for Effect implementation details"
    }
  }
}
```

Local `path` values may be relative to the declaring config, absolute, or use
`~/`. Git `repository` values accept Git URLs, host/path references, and GitHub
`owner/repo` shorthand; `branch` is optional. Both forms support optional
`description` and `hidden` fields.

- Only references with a `description` are advertised to agents in system context.
- `hidden: true` removes a reference from TUI `@` autocomplete only. It remains available to agents and by direct path.
- Reference directories are automatically allowed through the external-directory boundary; normal read/edit/tool permissions still apply.
- String shorthand is supported: use `"docs": "../docs"` for local paths or `"effect": "Effect-TS/effect"` for Git repositories.

## Agents

Two ways to define an agent. Use the file form for anything non-trivial.

### Inline (in `opencode.json`)

```json
{
  "agent": {
    "my-reviewer": {
      "description": "Reviews PRs for style violations.",
      "mode": "subagent",
      "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6",
      "permission": { "edit": "deny", "bash": "ask" },
      "prompt": "You are a strict PR reviewer..."
    }
  }
}
```

### File

```
.opencode/agent/my-reviewer.md      OR     .opencode/agents/my-reviewer.md
```

```markdown
---
description: Reviews PRs for style violations.
mode: subagent
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
permission:
  edit: deny
  bash: ask
---

You are a strict PR reviewer. Focus on...
```

The file body becomes the agent's `prompt`. Do not also put `prompt:` in the
frontmatter.

`mode` is one of `"primary"`, `"subagent"`, `"all"`.

Allowed top-level frontmatter fields: `name, model, variant, description, mode,
hidden, color, steps, options, permission, disable, temperature, top_p`. Any
unknown field is silently routed into `options`.

To disable a built-in agent: `agent: { build: { disable: true } }`, or in a
file, `disable: true` in frontmatter.

`default_agent` must point to a non-hidden, primary-mode agent.

### Built-in agents

opencode ships with `build`, `plan`, `general`, `explore`. Hidden internal agents:
`compaction`, `title`, `summary`. To override a built-in's fields, define the
same key in `agent: { <name>: { ... } }`.

## Commands

opencode's command loader scans for `**/*.md` inside command directories. The
file is named after the command, and lives directly inside the `command` folder:

```
.opencode/command/deploy.md
```

Frontmatter:

```markdown
---
description: One sentence describing what the command does.
agent: build
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
---

(command body in markdown: the prompt opencode runs, with $ARGUMENTS for the user's input)
```

- `template` is the command body — everything below the frontmatter — and is required: it is the prompt opencode runs when the command is invoked. Do not also put a `template:` key in the frontmatter.
- `$ARGUMENTS` is replaced with everything the user typed after the command; `$1`, `$2`, … pull individual positional arguments.
- Optional: `description`, `agent`, `model`, `variant`, `subtask`.

## Plugins

`plugin:` is an array. Each entry is one of:

```json
"plugin": [
  "opencode-gemini-auth",            // npm spec, latest
  "opencode-foo@1.2.3",              // npm spec, pinned
  "./local-plugin.ts",               // file path, relative to the declaring config
  "file:///abs/path/plugin.js",      // file URL
  ["opencode-bar", { "key": "val" }] // tuple form with options
]
```

Auto-discovered plugins (no config entry needed): any `*.ts` or `*.js` file in
`.opencode/plugin/` or `.opencode/plugins/`.

A plugin module exports `default` (or any named export) of type
`Plugin = (input: PluginInput, options?) => Promise<Hooks>`. The export is a
function, not a plain object literal, and the function returns an object
(return `{}` if there is nothing to register).

```ts
import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"

export default (async ({ client, project, directory, $ }) => {
  return {
    config: (cfg) => {
      // cfg is the live merged config; mutate fields here.
    },
    "tool.execute.before": async (input, output) => {
      // mutate output.args before the tool runs
    },
  }
}) satisfies Plugin
```

Hook surface (mutate `output` in place; return `void`):

- `event(input)`: every bus event
- `config(cfg)`: once on init with the merged config
- `chat.message`, `chat.params`, `chat.headers`
- `tool.execute.before`, `tool.execute.after`
- `tool.definition`
- `command.execute.before`
- `shell.env`
- `permission.ask`
- `experimental.chat.messages.transform`, `experimental.chat.system.transform`,
  `experimental.session.compacting`, `experimental.compaction.autocontinue`,
  `experimental.text.complete`

Special object-shaped (not callbacks): `tool: { my_tool: { ... } }`,
`auth: { ... }`, `provider: { ... }`.

## MCP servers

`mcp:` is an object keyed by server name. Each server is discriminated by
`type`:

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "playwright": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["npx", "-y", "@playwright/mcp"],
      "enabled": true,
      "env": { "BROWSER": "chromium" }
    },
    "github": {
      "type": "remote",
      "url": "https://...",
      "enabled": true,
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:GITHUB_TOKEN}" }
    },
    "old-server": { "enabled": false }
  }
}
```

`command` is an array of strings. `type` is required. Use `enabled: false` to
disable a server inherited from a parent config. String values such as header
tokens support `{env:VAR}` interpolation (and `{file:path}`); the shell-style
`${VAR}` is not substituted.

## Permissions

```json
"permission": {
  "edit": "deny",
  "bash": { "git *": "allow", "rm *": "deny", "*": "ask" },
  "external_directory": { "~/secrets/**": "deny", "*": "allow" }
}
```

Actions: `"allow"`, `"ask"`, `"deny"`.

Per-tool value forms: `"allow"` shorthand (treated as `{"*": "allow"}`), or an
object `{ pattern: action }`. Within an object, **insertion order matters**.
opencode evaluates the LAST matching rule, so put broad rules first and narrow
rules last.

`permission: "allow"` (a string at the top level) is shorthand for "allow
everything" and is rarely what the user wants.

Known permission keys: `read, edit, glob, grep, list, bash, task,
external_directory, todowrite, question, webfetch, websearch, lsp, doom_loop,
skill`. Some of these (`todowrite,
question, webfetch, websearch, doom_loop`) only accept a flat
action, not a per-pattern object.

`external_directory` patterns are filesystem paths (use `~/`, absolute paths,
or globs like `~/projects/**`).

Per-agent `permission:` overrides top-level `permission:`. Plan Mode lives on
the `plan` agent's permission ruleset (`edit: deny *`).

## Escape hatches

When a user's config is broken and opencode won't start, these env vars help:

- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG=1`: skip the project's local `opencode.json`
  and start from globals only. Run from the project directory, opencode loads,
  the user edits the broken file, then they restart without the flag.
- `OPENCODE_CONFIG=/path/to/file.json`: load an additional explicit config.
- `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT='{"$schema":"https://opencode.ai/config.json"}'`:
  inject inline JSON as a final local-scope merge.
- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_DEFAULT_PLUGINS=1`: skip default plugins.
- `OPENCODE_PURE=1`: skip external plugins entirely.
- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_EXTERNAL_SKILLS=1`,
  `OPENCODE_DISABLE_CLAUDE_CODE_SKILLS=1`: skip the external skill scans under
  `~/.claude/` and `~/.agents/`.

## When proposing edits

- Validate against the schema before writing. If you are unsure of a field's
  exact shape, or the field is not covered in this skill, fetch
  `https://opencode.ai/config.json` and read the schema rather than guessing.
- Preserve `$schema` and any existing fields the user did not ask to change.
- For agent, command, skill, and plugin definitions, prefer creating new files
  in the correct location over inlining everything in `opencode.json`.
- If the user's existing config is malformed, point them at the env-var escape
  hatches above so they can edit from inside opencode without breaking their
  session.
- After saving any config change, remind the user to quit and restart opencode
  — running sessions keep using the already-loaded config.

This document describes the monorepo organization of the OpenCode repository, including workspace structure, package categories, and inter-package dependencies. OpenCode uses Bun workspaces to manage multiple packages that together provide CLI tools, desktop applications, web interfaces, IDE extensions, and a managed cloud platform. For information about the architectural patterns and runtime behavior of these systems, see [Architecture Overview](#1.2). --- ## Workspace Organization OpenCode is organized as a monorepo with workspaces defined in the root configuration [bun.lock:4-28](). The repository contains 20+ packages distributed across several directories: | Directory | Purpose | Package Count | |---|---|---| | `packages/` | Core platform, UI components, SaaS Console, and services | 15+ packages | | `sdks/` | IDE integrations and extensions | 2+ packages | | Root | Main CLI package and build tooling | Workspace root | ### Workspace Configuration The root workspace [bun.lock:5-29]() defines shared dependencies and catalog versions that child packages inherit. The catalog system enforces consistent versioning across all packages for critical dependencies such as `typescript`, `solid-js`, `zod`, and others. ### Repository Package Hierarchy Diagram ```mermaid graph TB Root["Root Workspace

This document provides a high-level overview of the OpenCode system architecture, describing how the core components interact to provide an AI-powered coding assistant. It focuses on the backend infrastructure, API layers, core runtime components, and the transition toward the V2 architecture design across the monorepo packages. ## System Overview OpenCode is built as a modular, event-driven system centered around the `opencode` package that manages AI sessions, executes tools, and exposes a REST API. The architecture is deeply integrated with the `effect` library to manage side effects, dependency injection, and concurrency. This approach provides reliable orchestration of AI model calls, session management, and tool execution. The main runtime and services are implemented as `Effect` layers. It explains the command implementations, middleware pipeline, and error handling mechanisms. The focus is on the code-level understanding of how the CLI operates and delegates to specific commands such as `run`, `tui`, `serve`, `web`, `acp`, and others. For HTTP server functionality underpinning `serve` and `web`, see [HTTP Server & REST API](/2.6). For configuration details, see [Configuration System](/2.2). --- ## Entrypoint Architecture The core CLI entrypoint is `packages/opencode/src/index.ts`, which uses the `yargs` library for parsing command-line arguments, registering commands, and managing global options [packages/opencode/src/index.ts:1-45](). ### High-Level Flow Title: CLI Execution Pipeline ```mermaid graph TB Entry["index.ts Entrypoint"] Yargs["yargs CLI parser"] Middleware["Middleware pipeline"] Commands["Registered Commands"] ErrorHandler["Global error handler"] Entry --> Yargs Yargs --> Middleware Middleware --> Commands Commands --> ErrorHandler Middleware --> HeapStart["Heap.start()"] Commands --> Run["RunCommand (run)"] Commands --> TuiThread["TuiThreadCommand (tui)"] Commands --> Serve["ServeCommand (serve)"] Commands --> Web["WebCommand (web)"] Commands --> Acp["AcpCommand (acp)"] Commands --> Github["GithubCommand (github)"] Commands --> Other["Other commands..."] ErrorHandler --> FormatError["FormatError()"] ErrorHandler --> Exit["process.exit()"] ``` This architecture initializes the CLI parser, sets up global middleware for environment configuration, registers all commands, and gracefully handles errors to provide helpful user feedback. It supports three distinct modes [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/run.ts:5-11](): 1. **Non-interactive**: Sends a single prompt and streams events to stdout. 2. **Interactive local**: Boots an in-process server with a split-footer UI (`--mini`). 3. **Interactive attach**: Connects to an existing remote server (`--attach`). Key options include: - `--model` / `-m`: Specify `provider/model` [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/run.ts:165-169](). - `--agent`: Select specific agent configuration [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/run.ts:170-173](). - `--file` / `-f`: Attach files to the message [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/run.ts:180-185](). - `--format`: Choose between `default` (formatted) or `json` (raw events) [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/run.ts:174-179](). The command implements custom tool rendering, using `toolInlineInfo` to display tool execution status with icons (e.g., `⚙` for general tools, `✗` for failures) [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/run.ts:90-124](). Sources: [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/run.ts:1-230]() ### Serve & Web Commands Both `ServeCommand` and `WebCommand` initialize an OpenCode server. - `serve`: Starts a headless server listening on a specified port [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/serve.ts:6-23](). - `web`: Starts the server and automatically opens the web interface in the default browser using the `open` package [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/web.ts:31-84](). These commands utilize `resolveNetworkOptions` to parse hostname, port, and mDNS settings [packages/opencode/src/cli/web.ts:43](), [packages/opencode/src/cli/serve.ts:18](). Sources: [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/serve.ts:1-25](), [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/web.ts:31-85]() ### AcpCommand (`opencode acp`) The `AcpCommand` implements the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) server. It bridges JSON-RPC over `stdin`/`stdout` to an internal OpenCode server instance [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/acp.ts:9-73](). Implementation steps: 1. Starts the internal `Server` via `Server.listen(opts)` [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/acp.ts:25](). 2. Creates an `OpencodeClient` pointing to the local server [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/acp.ts:27-30](). 3. Wraps `process.stdin` and `process.stdout` into a `ndJsonStream` [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/acp.ts:32-55](). 4. Initializes `ACP.init` with the SDK and creates an `AgentSideConnection` [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/acp.ts:56-61](). Sources: [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/acp.ts:1-74]() ### StatsCommand (`opencode stats`) The `StatsCommand` aggregates and displays token usage and cost statistics from the local database [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/stats.ts:49-51](). - **Aggregation**: It queries the `SessionTable` via `Database.Service` to calculate totals for sessions, messages, costs, and token types (input, output, reasoning, cache) [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/stats.ts:83-147](). - **Filtering**: Supports filtering by `days` (e.g., last 30 days) and `project` [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/stats.ts:53-68](). - **Model Breakdown**: Can show top-N model usage including per-model cost and token metrics [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/stats.ts:184-203](). Sources: [packages/opencode/src/cli/cmd/stats.ts:1-230]() ### TuiThreadCommand (`opencode tui` or `opencode`) The `TuiThreadCommand` is responsible for launching the Terminal User Interface (TUI). The Configuration System in OpenCode manages hierarchical loading and merging of settings from various sources, maintaining clear precedence rules. It is responsible for loading configurations related to providers, agents, tools, permissions, plugins, and UI preferences, balancing flexibility between global, project, and runtime scopes. This page details the hierarchical configuration loading process, the `opencode.json` schema, and configuration precedence rules alongside their implementation, including the v2 design patterns. --- ## Configuration Sources and Precedence OpenCode supports multiple configuration sources that are merged into a unified configuration for runtime. The merging respects a strict order of precedence where later sources override specific keys from earlier ones but preserve non-conflicting keys. Configuration Loading Implementation The loading process is orchestrated inside `Config.Service` which provides reactive access to the merged config per project or instance context [packages/opencode/src/config/config.ts:124-135](). ### Data Flow: Config Resolution ```mermaid graph TD Start["Config.Service.get()"] Start --> Auth["Auth.Service.all()"] Auth --> RemoteLoop["fetchRemoteJson()"] RemoteLoop --> MergeRemote["mergeConfigConcatArrays()"] MergeRemote --> LoadGlobal["globalConfigFile()"] LoadGlobal --> MergeGlobal["mergeDeep()"] MergeGlobal --> LoadProject["ConfigPaths.projectFiles()"] LoadProject --> MergeProject["mergeDeep()"] MergeProject --> LoadDirs["ConfigPaths.directories()"] LoadDirs --> ProcessDirs["resolveLoadedPlugins()"] ProcessDirs --> Finalize["normalizeLoadedConfig()"] Finalize --> Return["Return Info Object"] ``` ### Merging Strategy The function `mergeConfigConcatArrays` is used specifically for fields like `instructions` to ensure that organizational defaults and user preferences are additive rather than subtractive [packages/opencode/src/config/config.ts:45-51](). For other fields, a deep merge is performed where later sources override earlier ones [packages/opencode/src/config/config.ts:41-43](). The filename (relative to the agents directory) becomes the agent's ID via `configEntryNameFromPath` [packages/opencode/src/config/agent.ts:22](). - **Frontmatter**: Defines metadata and properties which are parsed into `ConfigAgentV1.Info` [packages/opencode/src/config/agent.ts:26-29](). - **Body**: The markdown content is trimmed and used as the agent's `prompt` [packages/opencode/src/config/agent.ts:27](). **Sources:** [packages/opencode/src/config/agent.ts:11-59](), [packages/opencode/src/config/paths.ts:1-50]() --- ## Configuration API and V2 Evolution OpenCode exposes configuration management through its internal service and the generated V2 SDK. ### SDK Interface (`packages/sdk/js/src/v2/gen/sdk.gen.ts`) The V2 SDK provides a typed interface for interacting with the server's configuration system via the `config` and `globalConfig` namespaces. | Method | Description | |--------|-------------| | `config.get` | Retrieve current instance configuration [packages/sdk/js/src/v2/gen/sdk.gen.ts:21-22]() | | `config.update` | Update instance configuration [packages/sdk/js/src/v2/gen/sdk.gen.ts:25-26]() | | `globalConfig.get` | Retrieve global configuration [packages/sdk/js/src/v2/gen/sdk.gen.ts:79-80]() | | `globalConfig.update` | Update global configuration [packages/sdk/js/src/v2/gen/sdk.gen.ts:81-82]() | ### Service Implementation (`packages/opencode/src/config/config.ts`) - `Service.get()`: Returns the current `Info` state [packages/opencode/src/config/config.ts:125](). - `Service.update()`: Updates the configuration. The Session & Agent System is the core conversational runtime of OpenCode. It manages conversation threads (sessions), message and part structures, agent configurations (build, plan, explore, etc.), and the agentic execution loop that orchestrates LLM interactions with tools. Sessions use a descending ULID for `id` to ensure reverse-chronological sorting, facilitating recent-first display in UI components [packages/opencode/src/session/session.ts:37-38](), [packages/opencode/src/session/session.ts:60-121](). | Field | Type | Description | |--------------|-------------|----------------------------------------------------------------| | `id` | `SessionID` | Descending ULID ID uniquely identifying the session | | `slug` | `string` | URL-friendly identifier | | `projectID` | `string` | Links session to a specific project | | `workspaceID`| `string?` | Optionally links session to a workspace | | `parentID` | `string?` | For child/forked sessions referencing parent session | | `directory` | `string` | Path of working directory for the session | | `path` | `string?` | Optional project-relative path | | `title` | `string` | Session display title | | `agent` | `string?` | Agent name driving the session | | `model` | `object?` | Model and provider details used by the session | | `version` | `string` | Session versioning string | | `summary` | `object?` | Contains additions, deletions, files changed | | `cost` | `number` | Cost of session usage (tokens or monetary) | | `tokens` | `object` | Token usage broken down by input, output, reasoning, cache | | `share` | `object?` | Public share URL, if any | | `revert` | `object?` | Snapshot and diff information for revert operations | | `permission` | `Array` | Session-level permission ruleset overrides | | `metadata` | `object?` | Additional custom metadata, opaque | | `time` | `object` | Contains created, updated, compacting, and archived timestamps| ### Session Persistence Data Flow The following diagram shows how session lifecycle operations flow through the system layers from API to database. Assistant messages track token usage and costs to support analytics and billing [packages/opencode/src/session/message-v2.ts:80-85](), [packages/opencode/src/session/message-v2.ts:87-93](). ### Part Types Each part is discriminated by the `type` field with the following major types used in the system [packages/opencode/src/session/message-v2.ts:1-17](): | Part Type | Description | |--------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------| | `text` | Standard text content in the message | | `reasoning` | Blocks showing assistant's internal thought processes (for models supporting reasoning) | | `tool` | Represents a tool call with state and output details | | `file` | Attached files or media, with MIME type and URL | | `agent` | Reference to a subagent invocation within the conversation | | `compaction` | Marks where context compaction/summarization took place | | `snapshot` | Captures a snapshot state of the worktree at a given step | | `subtask` | Represents a task delegation or a subgoal handled recursively | This granularity allows tooling results, snapshots, and structured outputs to coexist in a single assistant response. The system handles media injection workarounds for providers (like OpenAI or Bedrock) that have limited support for media in tool results [packages/opencode/src/session/message-v2.ts:138-159](). **Sources:** - [packages/opencode/src/session/message-v2.ts:1-17]() - [packages/opencode/src/session/message-v2.ts:131-160]() --- ## Agent System Agents define the behavioral profile configuring how the LLM interacts with the environment, permissions, and tool usage. ### Agent Configurations Defined by the `Agent.Info` schema, an agent includes descriptive data, mode (e.g., "primary", "subagent"), permissions, and optional prompt and model override [packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts:35-56](). Out-of-the-box agents include: - **Build Agent**: The default primary agent executing permitted tools, allowing `question` and `plan_enter` permissions [packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts:141-156](). - **Plan Agent**: Specialized for architectural planning; disallows editing except in explicitly allowed plan files [packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts:157-182](). - **General Agent**: Intended for complex question answering and multitasking [packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts:183-198](). - **Explore Agent**: Optimized for codebase exploration, permissive with file read/search tools like `grep` and `glob` [packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts:199-208](). ### Permission Rulesets Permissions merge across three layers — global defaults, agent-specific rules, and user configuration — to create a final effective ruleset [packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts:120-153](). Key behaviors: - Default rules allow most actions but require explicit ask/deny on sensitive operations like `doom_loop` or access to external directories [packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts:120-127](). - Sensitive files like `.env` are set to `ask` by default to avoid accidental exposure [packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts:131-136](). - Agent-specific overrides may grant or restrict permissions, e.g., `plan` agent denies all edit except specific plan files [packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts:172-177](). **Sources:** - [packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts:35-153]() - [packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts:157-208]() --- ## Execution Loop & Context Management ### The Agent Loop The core conversational workflow is the agent loop which processes each assistant message generation in an event-driven streaming manner. This loop drives the LLM prompt-response cycles, tool executions, and updates to the session state [packages/opencode/src/session/prompt.ts:113-149](), [packages/opencode/src/session/processor.ts:98-115](). Steps: 1. **Start Processing**: The user prompt or assistant message triggers `SessionPrompt.loop`. 2. **LLM Completion Stream**: The configured LLM model streams text token-by-token and emits structured tool calls [packages/opencode/src/session/processor.ts:98-115](). 3. **Session Updates**: Intermediate assistant messages with their parts are saved to the database [packages/opencode/src/session/processor.ts:187-200](). 4. **Tool Calls**: Each tool call is dispatched to the `ToolRegistry`, which manages execution and returns results [packages/opencode/src/tool/registry.ts:138-164](). 5. **Result Updates**: Tool output parts update their tool call state with status and result [packages/opencode/src/session/processor.ts:160-184](). Title: "Agent Loop Execution (SessionProcessor)" ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant Loop as SessionPrompt.loop participant Proc as SessionProcessor.Service participant LLM as LLM.Service participant Tool as ToolRegistry.Service participant DB as Session.Service Loop->>Proc: create(input) Proc->>LLM: stream(message) LLM-->>Proc: stream text & tool calls Proc->>DB: save assistant message/parts loop For each Tool Call Proc->>Tool: execute tool call Tool-->>Proc: tool output Proc->>DB: update tool part state end Proc-->>Loop: return Result ("continue", "stop", or "compact") ``` **Sources:** - [packages/opencode/src/session/prompt.ts:113-149]() - [packages/opencode/src/session/processor.ts:160-184]() - [packages/opencode/src/session/processor.ts:98-115]() - [packages/opencode/src/session/processor.ts:187-200]() - [packages/opencode/src/tool/registry.ts:138-164]() ### Context Compaction & Truncation When the conversation context exceeds the model's maximum token window, the system performs automatic context compaction to summarize and prune content [packages/opencode/src/session/compaction.ts:131-150](). - **Overflow Detection**: Measures current token usage against configured context limits [packages/opencode/src/session/compaction.ts:168-178](). - **Turn-based Analysis**: Breaks session messages into user-assistant pairs (turns) and selects recent turns worth preserving based on a token budget [packages/opencode/src/session/compaction.ts:87-103](), [packages/opencode/src/session/compaction.ts:195-211](). - **Pruning**: Truncates excessive tool outputs to max characters (default 2,000) [packages/opencode/src/session/compaction.ts:30-31](). - **Context Injection**: Injects the summary into prompt parts to retain high-level session state while freeing token budget [packages/opencode/src/session/compaction.ts:52-60](). ### Retry Policy for LLM Calls A robust retry mechanism guards against transient API failures when interacting with LLM providers. This page documents the tool registry, built-in tools, the permission system gating tool execution at runtime in OpenCode, tool execution hooks, and file integrity mechanisms. It covers tool definition APIs, multi-layered permission evaluation, and techniques to ensure consistent file operations. --- ## Tool Definition API ### Overview All tools in OpenCode are defined via the `Tool.define` function. This utility abstracts JSON schema parameter validation, typed execution context injection, automatic output truncation, and error wrapping [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:151-169](). Tools are created as `Effect` generators to manage asynchronous dependencies like filesystem, LSP, or permission services. The registry normalizes these into a standard interface that the LLM can consume via JSON Schema [packages/opencode/src/tool/registry.ts:114-130](). ### Core Concepts - **Parameters**: Defined with `effect` schema and validated at runtime before execution. If validation fails, a `ToolInvalidArgumentsError` is returned to the LLM with specific details on how to rewrite the input [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:24-34](). - **Execute**: An async function that takes typed parameters and `Tool.Context`, returning an `ExecuteResult`. - **Context**: Carries runtime metadata such as session ID, agent info, and helpers for permission gating [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:36-46](). - **Output Truncation**: The wrapper automatically truncates output using `Truncate.Service` to prevent overwhelming the LLM context [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:131-144](). ### Tool.Context All tool executions receive a `Tool.Context`, which acts as the bridge between the tool implementation and the wider session state: | Property | Type | Description | | :---------- | :---------------------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------ | | `sessionID` | `SessionID` | The unique identifier for the current session [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:37](). | | `messageID` | `MessageID` | The ID of the message that triggered the tool call [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:38](). | | `agent` | `string` | The name of the agent executing the tool [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:39](). | | `abort` | `AbortSignal` | Signal to handle cancellation of the tool execution [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:40](). | | `metadata` | `Function` | Callback to update tool-specific metadata for the UI [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:44](). | | `ask` | `Function` | Primary interface for requesting permissions [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:45](). | ### Tool Registry The `ToolRegistry.Service` [packages/opencode/src/tool/registry.ts:81]() is responsible for discovering and managing all available tools. It aggregates: - Built-in tools (e.g., `read`, `edit`, `bash`) - Plugin-provided tools [packages/opencode/src/tool/registry.ts:114-169]() - Custom tools loaded from the `.opencode/tool` directory within the project [packages/opencode/src/tool/registry.ts:110-115]() The registry ensures that each tool has a unique ID, a description, and a JSON Schema for its parameters, which is crucial for LLM interaction [packages/opencode/src/tool/registry.ts:128-131](). #### Tool Definition and Initialization Tools are defined using `Tool.define(id, initEffect)` [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:157-169](). The `initEffect` is an `Effect` that resolves to a `DefWithoutID` object, containing the tool's description, parameters (as an `Effect/Schema` schema), and an `execute` function. The `wrap` function [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:99-148]() within `Tool.define` handles several cross-cutting concerns: - **Parameter Validation**: It decodes the input arguments against the defined `Schema` using `Schema.decodeUnknownEffect` [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:121](). If validation fails, it throws a `Tool.InvalidArgumentsError` [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:124-128](), providing a user-friendly error message to the LLM. - **Output Truncation**: It automatically truncates the tool's output using `Truncate.Service` to manage context window limits [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:131-144](). - **Execution Spans**: It wraps the `execute` call in an `Effect.withSpan` for observability and tracing [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:145-146](). #### Built-in Tools OpenCode includes a comprehensive set of built-in tools: | Tool ID | Implementation | Description | Parameters | | :------ | :------------- | :---------- | :--------- | | `read` | `ReadTool` [packages/opencode/src/tool/read.ts:64]() | Reads files/directories. ## Permission System ### Overview The permission system in OpenCode controls what actions agents can perform. It is implemented by the `Permission.Service` [packages/opencode/src/permission/index.ts:41]() and evaluates rulesets to determine if a tool call is `allow`, `deny`, or `ask` (requiring user confirmation). ### Permission Evaluation When a tool is executed, it calls `ctx.ask()` [packages/opencode/src/tool/tool.ts:45]() with the requested permission (e.g., `read`, `edit`, `bash`) and a pattern (e.g., a file path). The `Permission.Service` then evaluates this request against a hierarchy of rules: 1. **Agent-specific Rulesets**: Each agent (e.g., `build`, `plan`) has a default set of permissions defined in `Agent.Info` [packages/opencode/src/agent/agent.ts:35-55](). 2. **User-defined Rules**: Users can configure additional rules in `opencode.json` which are loaded and merged [packages/opencode/src/permission/index.ts:186-198](). 3. **Runtime Approvals**: If a permission is `ask`, the user can approve it "once" or "always". "Always" approvals are added to the `approved` state for the current session [packages/opencode/src/permission/index.ts:144-151](). The `evaluate` function [packages/opencode/src/permission/index.ts:28-37]() determines the final action by finding the last matching rule. If no explicit rule matches, the default action is `ask`. ### External Directory Protection A critical aspect of the permission system is protecting against unauthorized access to files outside the current project's worktree. The `assertExternalDirectoryEffect` function [packages/opencode/src/tool/external-directory.ts:10-50]() is used by file-system tools (`read`, `edit`, `write`, `apply_patch`) to check if a requested path is outside the project. If it is, it triggers a permission request for `external_directory`, requiring explicit user approval. #### Permission Evaluation Flow ```mermaid graph TD subgraph "Natural Language Space" tools. ### File Locking The `EditTool` uses a `Semaphore` to implement file-level locking [packages/opencode/src/tool/edit.ts:35-45](). When an `edit` operation is initiated on a `filePath`, a semaphore is acquired. This prevents multiple concurrent `edit` operations on the same file from causing race conditions or partial writes. ### Consistency Mechanisms 1. **Line Ending Normalization**: The `EditTool` detects the line ending style (`\n` or `\r\n`) and applies replacements using the detected style [packages/opencode/src/tool/edit.ts:22-34](). 2. **BOM Preservation**: Tools like `edit` and `apply_patch` utilize the `Bom` utility to handle Byte Order Marks (BOMs) [packages/opencode/src/tool/edit.ts:126-155](), [packages/opencode/src/tool/apply_patch.ts:115-118](). 3. **LSP Synchronization**: After modification, the `LSP.Service` is notified via `lsp.touchFile()` to re-index the changed file [packages/opencode/src/tool/edit.ts:115](). 4. **Binary Safety**: `ReadTool` "sniffs" initial bytes to determine if a file is binary [packages/opencode/src/tool/read.ts:182-200](). It refuses to read binary content as text to prevent context pollution. 5. **Instruction System**: The `Instruction.Service` [packages/opencode/src/session/instruction.ts:46]() manages project-specific instructions (e.g., `CLAUDE.md`). Tools integrate with this to ensure agents follow local coding standards. ### Background Subagents The `TaskTool` allows agents to launch subagents in the background using `BackgroundJob.Service` [packages/opencode/src/tool/task.ts:85](). - **Foreground**: Default; agent waits for subagent result. - **Background**: `background=true` launches asynchronously and returns immediately [packages/opencode/src/tool/task.ts:25-30](). - **Permission Derivation**: Subagents receive a subset of the parent's permissions via `deriveSubagentSessionPermission` [packages/opencode/src/agent/subagent-permissions.ts:10](). ### CodeMode Package The `packages/codemode` package provides a confined environment for code execution. - **Runtime Isolation**: The `CodeModeTool` [packages/opencode/src/tool/code-mode.ts]() uses this to run untrusted code safely. - **Tool Access**: Code running in CodeMode can be granted limited access to host tools via `tool-runtime.ts` [packages/codemode/src/tool-runtime.ts](). - **Verification**: Uses signature verification to ensure code hasn't been tampered with before execution [packages/codemode/test/signature.test.ts](). This page documents the HTTP server implementation and REST API architecture that powers OpenCode's networked functionality. The server provides a comprehensive REST API for managing sessions, projects, configurations, and real-time AI interactions using the Effect-based `HttpApi` framework. ## Purpose and Scope The HTTP server serves as the central networked interface to OpenCode's core functionality. It exposes endpoints for: - **Session Lifecycle**: CRUD operations on sessions, message history, and AI prompting [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/groups/session.ts:79-105](). - **Real-time Updates**: Event streaming via Server-Sent Events (SSE) for UI synchronization [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/groups/event.ts:1-10](). - **Provider Management**: Discovery of LLM models and credential configuration [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/groups/provider.ts:1-10](). - **System Control**: Health checks, upgrades, and global instance disposal [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/groups/control.ts:1-10](). - **Terminal Integration**: WebSocket-based pseudo-terminal (PTY) access for remote shell execution [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/groups/pty.ts:1-10](). Sources: [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/groups/session.ts:79-105](), [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/groups/event.ts:1-10](), [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/groups/provider.ts:1-10](), [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/groups/control.ts:1-10](), [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/groups/pty.ts:1-10]() ## Server Architecture OpenCode uses a modern, type-safe server architecture built on the **Effect** ecosystem. The server logic is defined using `HttpApi`, which enables automatic OpenAPI generation and unified dependency injection across all routes [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/api.ts:54-75](). The main server entry is in `packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts` which sets up listeners and integrates the HTTP API routes [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:139-151](). The server supports two primary execution modes: 1. **Network Mode**: An actual HTTP server bound to a TCP port, using `HttpRouter.serve` to bind the route handlers [packages/opencode/test/server/httpapi-session.test.ts:49-55](). 2. **Local Transport Mode**: A "web handler" interface that runs request handling directly without network overhead, useful for internal calls and testing [packages/opencode/test/server/httpapi-ui.test.ts:53-75](). ### Request Flow and Middleware The server defines a layered middleware stack that applies common functionality like authentication, error handling, CORS, compression, and workspace routing. These groups correspond to different concerns and prefixes: | Path Prefix | Functionality | Implementation | |---|---|---| | `/global` | Global system status, events, logs | `globalHandlers` [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:90-90]() | | `/auth`, `/log` | Control plane and authentication | `controlHandlers` [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:86-86]() | | `/session`, `/file`| Session management, filesystem ops | `sessionHandlers`, `fileHandlers` [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:99-99](), [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:89-89]() | | `/event` | Real-time server-sent event streaming | `eventHandlers` [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:84-84]() | | `/doc` | OpenAPI specification JSON | Exposed via `OpenApi.toSpec` [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:151-151]() | Sources: [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:82-151]() ## Middleware and Lifecycle ### Authentication Authentication and authorization are enforced through dedicated layers: - `authorizationLayer`: Implements Basic Auth using credentials configured via environment variables (`OPENCODE_SERVER_USERNAME` and `OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD`) [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/authorization.ts:118-132](). - `ptyConnectAuthorizationLayer`: Specialized authorization middleware for PTY WebSocket connections using one-time tickets [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/authorization.ts:134-150](). - `serverAuthorizationLayer`: Used for global server-level routes and applied to `RootHttpApi` [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:139-139](). Authorization tokens may be passed via query parameter `auth_token` or HTTP Basic Auth header. Unauthorized access triggers `401 Unauthorized` with appropriate `WWW-Authenticate` headers [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/authorization.ts:12-83](). Sources: [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/authorization.ts:8-150](), [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:136-139]() ### CORS Configuration Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is configured via a middleware wrapping `HttpMiddleware.cors`. It uses a whitelist logic in `isAllowedCorsOrigin` that checks origins against configured allowed origins [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:121-129](). A small accompanying middleware `corsVaryFix` ensures compliant response headers for varying CORS origins [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/cors-vary.ts:1-10](). Sources: [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:121-129](), [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/cors-vary.ts:1-10]() ### Workspace Routing The `workspaceRoutingLayer` middleware manages routing requests to local or remote workspaces. - It extracts workspace and directory info from URL queries or headers [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/workspace-routing.ts:22-30](). - If a remote workspace is specified, it proxies the request transparently to remote URLs using an `HttpApiProxy` [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/workspace-routing.ts:113-146](). - Ensures context typing for instance services to support session isolation across project directories [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/workspace-routing.ts:52-62](). Sources: [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/workspace-routing.ts:22-62](), [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/workspace-routing.ts:113-146]() ### Error Handling Robust error handling is provided through: - An `errorLayer` catches unhandled exceptions, returning a sanitized 500 Internal Server Error with a unique error reference [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/error.ts:9-36](). - A `schemaErrorLayer` specifically handles schema validation errors from request bodies or parameters, converting them into 400 Bad Request responses [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/schema-error.ts:1-10](). Sources: [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/error.ts:9-36](), [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/middleware/schema-error.ts:1-10]() ## Real-time Transport Modes ### Server-Sent Events (SSE) The server supports real-time event streaming over SSE through the `EventApi` group. This multiplexes different event types related to sessions, projects, and global state [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/api.ts:81-81](). The `eventHandlers` bridge internal event buses to SSE HTTP responses, providing clients with incremental updates for UI synchronization [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:84-84](). Sources: [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/api.ts:81-81](), [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:84-84]() ### WebSockets (PTY) Interactive terminal sessions are managed under the `PtyConnectApi` namespace. - Clients first request a one-time connection ticket at `/pty/{ptyID}/token` [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/handlers/pty.ts:144-150](). - Using the ticket, WebSocket upgrade requests are accepted at `/pty/{ptyID}/connect` [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/handlers/pty.ts:163-200](). - `WebSocketTracker` monitors all active PTY WebSocket connections for graceful shutdown [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/websocket-tracker.ts:1-10](). Sources: [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/handlers/pty.ts:144-200](), [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/websocket-tracker.ts:1-10]() ## OpenAPI Specification The HTTP REST API is formally defined using the `effect/unstable/httpapi` framework. This provides: - **Typed Route Definitions**: The `RootHttpApi`, `InstanceHttpApi`, and other groups define routes with attached JSON schemas [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/api.ts:54-75](). - **OpenAPI Doc Generation**: The API specification can be dynamically generated via `OpenApi.fromApi(PublicApi)` [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/server.ts:151-151](). - **Legacy Compatibility**: A transformation layer in `matchLegacyOpenApi` normalizes schemas (e.g., stripping optional nulls, fixing circular references) to support existing SDK generation [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/public.ts:82-145](). - **Query Parameter Overrides**: Several query parameters have explicit schema overrides to ensure primitive types (numbers, booleans) in the generated SDK [packages/opencode/src/server/routes/instance/httpapi/public.ts:58-74](). # Plugins

Write your own plugins to extend OpenCode.

Plugins allow you to extend OpenCode by hooking into various events and customizing behavior. You can create plugins to add new features, integrate with external services, or modify OpenCode’s default behavior.

For examples, check out the [plugins](/docs/ecosystem#plugins) created by the community.

---

## [Use a plugin](#use-a-plugin)

There are two ways to load plugins.

---

### [From local files](#from-local-files)

Place JavaScript or TypeScript files in the plugin directory.

-   `.opencode/plugins/` - Project-level plugins
-   `~/.config/opencode/plugins/` - Global plugins

Files in these directories are automatically loaded at startup.

---

### [From npm](#from-npm)

Specify npm packages in your config file.

opencode.json

```
{  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",  "plugin": ["opencode-helicone-session", "opencode-wakatime", "@my-org/custom-plugin"]}
```

Both regular and scoped npm packages are supported.

Browse available plugins in the [ecosystem](/docs/ecosystem#plugins).

---

### [How plugins are installed](#how-plugins-are-installed)

**npm plugins** are installed automatically using Bun at startup. Packages and their dependencies are cached in `~/.cache/opencode/node_modules/`.

**Local plugins** are loaded directly from the plugin directory. To use external packages, you must create a `package.json` within your config directory (see [Dependencies](#dependencies)), or publish the plugin to npm and [add it to your config](/docs/config#plugins).

---

### [Load order](#load-order)

Plugins are loaded from all sources and all hooks run in sequence. The load order is:

1.  Global config (`~/.config/opencode/opencode.json`)
2.  Project config (`opencode.json`)
3.  Global plugin directory (`~/.config/opencode/plugins/`)
4.  Project plugin directory (`.opencode/plugins/`)

Duplicate npm packages with the same name and version are loaded once. However, a local plugin and an npm plugin with similar names are both loaded separately.

---

## [Create a plugin](#create-a-plugin)

A plugin is a **JavaScript/TypeScript module** that exports one or more plugin functions. Each function receives a context object and returns a hooks object.

---

### [Dependencies](#dependencies)

Local plugins and custom tools can use external npm packages. Add a `package.json` to your config directory with the dependencies you need.

.opencode/package.json

```
{  "dependencies": {    "shescape": "^2.1.0"  }}
```

OpenCode runs `bun install` at startup to install these. Your plugins and tools can then import them.

.opencode/plugins/my-plugin.ts

```
import { escape } from "shescape"
export const MyPlugin = async (ctx) => {  return {    "tool.execute.before": async (input, output) => {      if (input.tool === "bash") {        output.args.command = escape(output.args.command)      }    },  }}
```

---

### [Basic structure](#basic-structure)

.opencode/plugins/example.js

```
export const MyPlugin = async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => {  console.log("Plugin initialized!")
  return {    // Hook implementations go here  }}
```

The plugin function receives:

-   `project`: The current project information.
-   `directory`: The current working directory.
-   `worktree`: The git worktree path.
-   `client`: An opencode SDK client for interacting with the AI.
-   `$`: Bun’s [shell API](https://bun.com/docs/runtime/shell) for executing commands.

---

### [TypeScript support](#typescript-support)

For TypeScript plugins, you can import types from the plugin package:

my-plugin.ts

```
import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"
export const MyPlugin: Plugin = async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => {  return {    // Type-safe hook implementations  }}
```

---

### [Events](#events)

Plugins can subscribe to events as seen below in the Examples section. Here is a list of the different events available.

#### [Command Events](#command-events)

-   `command.executed`

#### [File Events](#file-events)

-   `file.edited`
-   `file.watcher.updated`

#### [Installation Events](#installation-events)

-   `installation.updated`

#### [LSP Events](#lsp-events)

-   `lsp.client.diagnostics`
-   `lsp.updated`

#### [Message Events](#message-events)

-   `message.part.removed`
-   `message.part.updated`
-   `message.removed`
-   `message.updated`

#### [Permission Events](#permission-events)

-   `permission.asked`
-   `permission.replied`

#### [Server Events](#server-events)

-   `server.connected`

#### [Session Events](#session-events)

-   `session.created`
-   `session.compacted`
-   `session.deleted`
-   `session.diff`
-   `session.error`
-   `session.idle`
-   `session.status`
-   `session.updated`

#### [Todo Events](#todo-events)

-   `todo.updated`

#### [Shell Events](#shell-events)

-   `shell.env`

#### [Tool Events](#tool-events)

-   `tool.execute.after`
-   `tool.execute.before`

#### [TUI Events](#tui-events)

-   `tui.prompt.append`
-   `tui.command.execute`
-   `tui.toast.show`

---

## [Examples](#examples)

Here are some examples of plugins you can use to extend opencode.

---

### [Send notifications](#send-notifications)

Send notifications when certain events occur:

.opencode/plugins/notification.js

```
export const NotificationPlugin = async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => {  return {    event: async ({ event }) => {      // Send notification on session completion      if (event.type === "session.idle") {        await $`osascript -e 'display notification "Session completed!" with title "opencode"'`      }    },  }}
```

We are using `osascript` to run AppleScript on macOS. Here we are using it to send notifications.

Note

If you’re using the OpenCode desktop app, it can send system notifications automatically when a response is ready or when a session errors.

---

### [.env protection](#env-protection)

Prevent opencode from reading `.env` files:

.opencode/plugins/env-protection.js

```
export const EnvProtection = async ({ project, client, $, directory, worktree }) => {  return {    "tool.execute.before": async (input, output) => {      if (input.tool === "read" && output.args.filePath.includes(".env")) {        throw new Error("Do not read .env files")      }    },  }}
```

---

### [Inject environment variables](#inject-environment-variables)

Inject environment variables into all shell execution (AI tools and user terminals):

.opencode/plugins/inject-env.js

```
export const InjectEnvPlugin = async () => {  return {    "shell.env": async (input, output) => {      output.env.MY_API_KEY = "secret"      output.env.PROJECT_ROOT = input.cwd    },  }}
```

---

### [Custom tools](#custom-tools)

Plugins can also add custom tools to opencode:

.opencode/plugins/custom-tools.ts

```
import { type Plugin, tool } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"
export const CustomToolsPlugin: Plugin = async (ctx) => {  return {    tool: {      mytool: tool({        description: "This is a custom tool",        args: {          foo: tool.schema.string(),        },        async execute(args, context) {          const { directory, worktree } = context          return `Hello ${args.foo} from ${directory} (worktree: ${worktree})`        },      }),    },  }}
```

The `tool` helper creates a custom tool that opencode can call. It takes a Zod schema function and returns a tool definition with:

-   `description`: What the tool does
-   `args`: Zod schema for the tool’s arguments
-   `execute`: Function that runs when the tool is called

Your custom tools will be available to opencode alongside built-in tools.

Note

If a plugin tool uses the same name as a built-in tool, the plugin tool takes precedence.

---

### [Logging](#logging)

Use `client.app.log()` instead of `console.log` for structured logging:

.opencode/plugins/my-plugin.ts

```
export const MyPlugin = async ({ client }) => {  await client.app.log({    body: {      service: "my-plugin",      level: "info",      message: "Plugin initialized",      extra: { foo: "bar" },    },  })}
```

Levels: `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`. See [SDK documentation](https://opencode.ai/docs/sdk) for details.

---

### [Compaction hooks](#compaction-hooks)

Customize the context included when a session is compacted:

.opencode/plugins/compaction.ts

```
import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"
export const CompactionPlugin: Plugin = async (ctx) => {  return {    "experimental.session.compacting": async (input, output) => {      // Inject additional context into the compaction prompt      output.context.push(`## Custom Context
Include any state that should persist across compaction:- Current task status- Important decisions made- Files being actively worked on`)    },  }}
```

The `experimental.session.compacting` hook fires before the LLM generates a continuation summary. Use it to inject domain-specific context that the default compaction prompt would miss.

You can also replace the compaction prompt entirely by setting `output.prompt`:

.opencode/plugins/custom-compaction.ts

```
import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"
export const CustomCompactionPlugin: Plugin = async (ctx) => {  return {    "experimental.session.compacting": async (input, output) => {      // Replace the entire compaction prompt      output.prompt = `You are generating a continuation prompt for a multi-agent swarm session.
Summarize:1. The current task and its status2. Which files are being modified and by whom3. Any blockers or dependencies between agents4. The next steps to complete the work
Format as a structured prompt that a new agent can use to resume work.`    },  }}
```

When `output.prompt` is set, it completely replaces the default compaction prompt. The `output.context` array is ignored in this case.

input.question: How do subagents work in opencode? Are they separate processes, threads, or just separate sessions in the same process? How does the task tool create subagents? Look at packages/opencode/src/tool/task.ts and the subagent session creation code. Specifically: is a subagent a separate OS process running opencode, or is it an in-process LLM call with different settings? Are plugins loaded per subagent session?

Subagents in OpenCode are not separate OS processes or threads; they operate as separate sessions within the same process, essentially as in-process LLM calls with different settings. The `TaskTool` in `packages/opencode/src/tool/task.ts` is responsible for creating and managing these subagent sessions. Plugins are loaded per subagent session, as indicated by the permission handling during session creation.

## Subagent Mechanism

Subagents are specialized AI assistants that can be invoked by primary agents or directly by the user via `@` mentions.  They are configured with custom prompts, models, and tool access permissions. 

### Session Creation

When a subagent is invoked, either by a primary agent using the `task` tool or directly by the user, a new session is created for it.  This session is distinct from the parent session but runs within the same OpenCode process.  The `TaskTool`'s `execute` method in `packages/opencode/src/tool/task.ts` handles this creation. 

The `TaskTool` defines parameters for creating a subagent, including `description`, `prompt`, and `subagent_type`.  It also allows for resuming a previous subagent session by providing a `task_id`. 

The core logic for creating a new session for the subagent is found in the `TaskTool`'s `run` function:

This code snippet shows that if a `task_id` is provided, it attempts to retrieve an existing session.  Otherwise, it creates a new session using `sessions.create()`, associating it with the parent session via `parentID`. 

### In-Process LLM Calls

Subagents are essentially in-process LLM calls with different settings.  The `ops.prompt` function is called with the new session's `sessionID`, `model`, `variant`, and `agent` settings.  This indicates that the LLM interaction for the subagent occurs within the same process as the main OpenCode application.

### Plugin Loading and Permissions

Plugins are loaded per subagent session through the permission system. When a subagent session is created, its permissions are derived from the parent session's deny rules and the subagent's own defined permissions.  The `deriveSubagentSessionPermission` function in `packages/opencode/src/agent/subagent-permissions.ts` explicitly constructs the permission ruleset for the child session.  This ruleset includes permissions for tools like `todowrite` and `task`.  The `childToolDenies` array in `packages/opencode/src/tool/task.ts` further refines which tools are available to the subagent based on its configuration.  This granular control over permissions effectively means that plugins (tools) are enabled or disabled on a per-subagent-session basis.

## Notes

The documentation in `packages/web/src/content/docs/agents.mdx` provides a high-level overview of primary agents and subagents, their types, and usage, confirming that subagents are specialized assistants.  The `packages/opencode/src/tool/task.txt` file offers usage notes for the `task` tool, emphasizing that each agent invocation starts with a fresh context unless a `task_id` is provided to resume a session.  This reinforces the idea of subagents operating as distinct sessions. The e2e tests in `packages/app/e2e/regression/subagent-child-navigation.spec.ts` also demonstrate the creation and navigation between parent and child subagent sessions, further supporting the session-based model.

input.question: How does the Plugin.Service work? Are plugins loaded globally once at startup and shared across all sessions (including subagent sessions)? Or is each plugin loaded independently per session/process? Look at how the plugin system initializes in packages/opencode/src/plugin/ and how plugin hooks are called in the session processing pipeline. Is there any state isolation between sessions?

parts.output:
The `Plugin.Service` in `anomalyco/opencode` manages the loading, initialization, and execution of plugins. Plugins are loaded per session or process, not globally, ensuring state isolation between sessions. The system distinguishes between internal plugins, which are built-in, and external plugins, which are loaded from configuration or local files.

### Plugin Initialization and Loading
The core of the plugin system resides in `packages/opencode/src/plugin/index.ts` . The `Service` class, specifically its `layer` constant, is responsible for initializing plugins .

1.  **Internal Plugins**: These are built-in plugins directly imported into the codebase . They are loaded first unless `flags.disableDefaultPlugins` is true . Examples include `CodexAuthPlugin` and `CopilotAuthPlugin` .
2.  **External Plugins**: These are specified in the configuration (`cfg.plugin_origins`) or loaded from local files . The `PluginLoader.loadExternal` function handles the loading of these plugins . This process involves resolving the plugin's target, checking compatibility, and dynamically importing the module .
    *   External plugins are loaded in parallel, but their activation is sequential to maintain deterministic command, route, and side-effect order .
    *   If a plugin fails to load or initialize, an error is logged, and the system attempts to continue loading other plugins .

The `PluginLoader` namespace in `packages/opencode/src/plugin/loader.ts` defines the types and functions for planning, resolving, and loading plugins .

### Plugin Hooks and Session Processing
Plugins interact with the system through "hooks" . The `Plugin.Service` provides a `trigger` method to execute these hooks .

When a hook is triggered, the `trigger` method iterates through all registered hooks and executes the corresponding function . This allows plugins to intercept and modify behavior at various points in the session processing pipeline.

### State Isolation
Plugins are loaded and initialized within the context of an `InstanceState` . This `InstanceState` is created per session or process, meaning that each session gets its own set of plugin hooks and associated state . This design ensures that plugins are loaded independently per session/process, providing state isolation. The `SessionExecution` and `SessionStore` are process-global, but other components like `SessionRunner`, catalog, and tool registry are cached per `Location` .

The `PluginV2.Service` in `packages/core/src/plugin.ts` also provides methods to `add`, `remove`, and `wait` for plugins, further indicating a dynamic, per-instance management of plugins rather than a global, static load . The `PluginV2` tests confirm that plugins can be added, replaced, and removed dynamically, affecting the state of agents within a specific context .

## Notes
The documentation files in `packages/web/src/content/docs/`  provide user-facing information about how to use and install plugins, including load order and dependency management. While these documents confirm that plugins are loaded from various sources (global config, project config, global plugin directory, project plugin directory) , the core implementation in `packages/opencode/src/plugin/index.ts`  and `packages/opencode/src/plugin/loader.ts`  clarifies that this loading happens within an `InstanceState` context, ensuring per-session isolation.
